endorsements.quote: Fairness-aware data augmentation and adversarial debiasing can expand representational diversity within training datasets, while transfer learning enables the adaptation of robust models to rare or under-sampled pathogens ( Khosravi et al., 2025 ; Mohammed Aarif et al., 2025 ).

Systematic evaluation of factual accuracy has been proposed as a safeguard against such spurious results, ensuring that AI-generated insights are not only internally consistent but also biologically credible ( Wysocka et al., 2024 ).

unlisted_practices: Embed mutation, horizontal gene transfer, and adaptive landscape dynamics explicitly into generative AI models for antimicrobial resistance prediction.
Validate generative AI resistance predictions iteratively through experimental evolution and real-world surveillance.
Test AI-proposed mutational pathways against real-world phenotypic outcomes before relying on them.
Ensure explainability methods demonstrate biological plausibility by linking genotypic markers to phenotypic resistance outcomes.
Combine rule-based inference with machine learning in hybrid systems to embed established biological knowledge.
Openly disclose training data quality and adhere to regulatory standards to safeguard against dual-use risks.
Integrate biosafety and regulatory compliance at the design stage of generative AI for microbiology.
Use causally informed frameworks to model bias propagation and identify structural confounders in microbial datasets.
Incorporate phylogenetic relationships as structural priors to constrain generative model outputs.
Make equity a measurable and auditable property of microbial AI systems.
Establish transparency, accountability, and global data-sharing mechanisms to prevent inequitable predictive infrastructures.

screen.reason: This is a perspective piece discussing imperatives for the use of generative AI in antimicrobial resistance, focusing on explainability, biosafety, and data equity.
